headline: The Water Went Green on the Ledge — and Something's Coming Behind It
subhead: Stripers are still stacked on the Southwest Ledge, but the sharks are working them hard, and the first bonito are knocking on the door from Watch Hill.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out to the Southwest Ledge Tuesday morning before first light, flat calm, and the water had that cold, green weight to it that tells you the current's about to start pulling hard. You get a feel for that out here after enough years — the air changes, the swell tightens up, and you know the tide's building toward something. With the new moon coming August 12, that's exactly what's happening. The current through the rips is starting to load up, and everything that's been sitting loose and lazy all July is about to get pushed around with a purpose.

The bass are still here, and they haven't gone anywhere — that's the one constant on this island in August. I've been marking good concentrations of stripers from 40 to 60 feet on the northwest corner of the Ledge, right where the structure drops off into that mixing water. Live eels on the drift, slow-trolled just off bottom on the last two hours of the ebb, have been the most consistent producer. I pulled a 34-pounder off there Wednesday on an eel fished behind a three-way rig with just enough lead to keep it ticking bottom without snagging up. The North Rip has been holding fish too, mostly on the west side where the current stacks bait against the drop — tube and worm still works there if you want to cover water, but the eel bite at night has been better than anything in daylight.

Here's the part I need every one of you to hear, because it matters more this year than it has in a long time. We're seeing heavy brown shark activity working the same structure the bass are holding on, and the mortality rate on released fish that get worked by sharks after the fight is brutal — we're talking somewhere near 90 percent of those fish don't make it. If you're fighting a good bass on the Ledge or around the North Rip this week, get it to the boat fast. Don't play it out on light drag just to enjoy the fight. Use heavier gear than you think you need, get the fish up, and if you see shadows working under the boat, consider just not fighting that next one at all. This isn't a scare tactic — it's what's actually happening out there right now, and it's specific to this stretch of water. I'd rather you catch fewer bass and know they swam away clean than land three and lose two to sharks before they ever get a hook out.

On the bonito front — we flagged this last week, said the new moon current would be the trigger, and it's already happening. Watch Hill and the Sakonnet stretch have had a legitimate bonito push moving through, and that leading edge is close enough now that I expect the first committed sightings inside Block Island Sound any day. Nothing confirmed on our own water yet as of this morning, but the signs are all there — the water temperature's holding in that comfortable summer range, bait's getting pushed hard through the rips as the tidal range builds toward the 12th, and that's precisely the recipe that flips this fishery on fast once it starts. If you want to be ready, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a Deadly Dick or a small Albie Snax on standby anytime you're out around the Southeast Light structure or drifting bait through the mouth of the Great Salt Pond. When they show, they show suddenly, and you want to already have a rod in your hand.

Bluefish have been a mixed bag — some real gators mixed in with the bass on the Ledge, taking the same eels, but the consistent chopper action has been off the East Grounds on diamond jigs, 2 to 3 ounces, worked with a fast retrieve through the bait schools. Fluke fishing off the island has been steady but unspectacular — the usual mix of shorts with the occasional keeper in the 20-foot range off the breakwater and around Cormorant Cove, white Gulp swimming mullet on 3/4-ounce bucktails doing the damage on the drift. Nothing to write home about, but a fun way to fill a cooler while you wait for something bigger. Porgies remain thick around the docks and the shallower rock piles inside the Sound — bloodworms and squid strips on high-low rigs, easy family fishing if you've got kids aboard who want steady action. Blackfish season's still closed here, so leave the crabs at the shop for now.

Looking ahead, I'd put my money on the next five days being about watching, not just fishing. The tidal range is going to keep building into Wednesday's new moon, and that's when I expect this whole thing to sharpen up — bass bite tightening on the structure, and a real shot at that first bonito or albie showing up inside the Sound. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd want it to be Tuesday or Wednesday on a strong outgoing tide at the Ledge, working eels early and keeping a bonito rod rigged the whole time just in case. Handle your bass fast, keep the fight short, and watch the water — it's about to start telling you something different than it has all summer.
